questions.q: What is a site-to-site VPN in the context of connecting an on-premises network to a cloud VNet/VPC?
options: A dedicated private circuit that never touches the public internet
An encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet between an on-premises VPN device and a cloud VPN gateway
A DNS-only configuration with no encryption or network-layer connectivity
A feature that exists only on AWS, with no Azure equivalent
questions.explain: A site-to-site VPN is an IPsec tunnel over the public internet — fast and inexpensive to stand up, but subject to the internet's variable throughput and latency.

questions.q: Why would an enterprise provision an ExpressRoute circuit or a Direct Connect connection instead of relying solely on a site-to-site VPN?
options: ExpressRoute and Direct Connect are the only options that support encryption
A VPN cannot be configured to connect to more than one VNet or VPC
ExpressRoute and Direct Connect are always cheaper and faster to provision than a VPN
Workloads needing predictable, guaranteed bandwidth and lower latency require a dedicated circuit that bypasses the public internet
questions.explain: ExpressRoute and Direct Connect provide dedicated, private connectivity with consistent throughput and latency, at higher cost and longer provisioning time — exactly what latency-sensitive or high-volume workloads need.

questions.q: What is the realistic hybrid identity pattern most enterprises follow, according to this lesson?
options: Extend the existing on-premises Active Directory into the cloud via Microsoft Entra Connect or AWS Directory Service, rather than standing up a second, independent directory
Abandon Active Directory entirely and manage all identities natively in the cloud provider's console
Maintain two fully independent directories — one on-prem, one in the cloud — with no synchronization
Require every user to have separate, unrelated credentials for on-prem and cloud systems
questions.explain: The realistic pattern is extension, not duplication — Microsoft Entra Connect and AWS Directory Service (AD Connector or Managed Microsoft AD) extend the existing on-prem AD into cloud identity rather than replacing it.

questions.q: What problem does the hub-and-spoke topology solve once an enterprise has multiple on-prem sites and multiple cloud VNets/VPCs?
options: It increases the number of point-to-point connections needed between every site and every network
It removes the need for any network connectivity between on-prem and cloud
It centralizes shared connectivity in one hub so spokes connect only to the hub, avoiding unmanageable point-to-point growth
It replaces the need for identity extension entirely
questions.explain: Hub-and-spoke centralizes the VPN gateway or ExpressRoute/Direct Connect termination and shared services in a hub; every spoke peers only to the hub, so connectivity scales without a point-to-point explosion.

questions.q: What is AWS Directory Service's AD Connector designed to do?
options: Proxy authentication requests from AWS back to an existing on-premises Active Directory, rather than duplicating the directory in AWS
Create an entirely independent directory inside AWS with no relationship to the on-premises forest
Replace Direct Connect as a network connectivity option
Function only as a DNS resolver for AWS VPCs
questions.explain: AD Connector proxies authentication back to the existing on-premises AD, keeping it the single authoritative identity source instead of creating a separate directory to maintain.
